speechtext: I am sure the minister has material in front of him on the basis of which he can make a statement on this $10 million item. I think we should have that statement.

Perhaps I should make my general statement here, then, because much of it revolves around the trade commissioner service which recently spent a very profitable seven weeks touring Canada in the interests of trade and the general economic health of the country. I will not deal with the Kennedy round at this time.
On June 8 I was privileged to meet the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Essex West. The estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce were reviewed very thoroughly at that time. I dealt with the current and projected plans of the department. The proceedings of that meeting have been printed and published, so I do not intend to burden hon. members with a repetition of the department's achievements and intentions as of that day. However, we have been moving forward, and it might be useful if I were to comment briefly upon certain activities which I believe might be of interest to the committee.
Following an almost unprecedented expansion in exports in 1966, sales abroad have continued to advance strongly in the current year. To emphasize the vital importance to the Canadian economy of sustaining strong export growth, a target of $11.25 billion was set last fall as an export objective for Canada's centennial year. Although considered at the time to be a particularly stiff challenge, this target has received the full endorsation and support of the export community.
2152	COMMONS
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Developments so far suggest that these high aspirations are in fact well on the way to realization. Notwithstanding the prevalence of less pressing demand conditions this year in some of our principal export markets, particularly the United States and the European community, figures for the first five months of the year show exports up 16.5 per cent or $650 million compared with the same period of 1966. This means that about two thirds of the projected increase for the year has already been achieved.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
The figures for the month of May show total exports of $1,066.7 million, as against $932.9 million for May, 1966, an increase of 14.3 per cent. This includes substantial increases in exports to the United Kingdom, other commonwealth countries and the United States. The figure for the United States, for example, for May is up by 18.2 per cent. For the months of January through May the total amount of our exports is $4,593.3 million as against $3,943.1 million for the period of January through May, 1966, a total full increase of 16.5 per cent.
Even allowing for a diminution in the strength of some of the forces contributing to this early-year expansion, there is good likelihood that the $11.25 billion target will be realized and possibly exceeded. This will represent a creditable showing indeed in a year characterized by significantly slower growth in world trade as a whole.
I have indicated, without going into the Kennedy round negotiations, what steps we plan to make the results available to the business community in Canada. The statistics have been circulated to trade associations and have been sent out directly from my office to some 153 companies. The export advisory board has been invited to Ottawa; they will arrive here early next week. We shall brief them and ask them to carry the message back to their communities. In addition, we plan a series of regional or sectional seminars in various parts of Canada-some in co-operation with provincial authorities concerned with trade, some in collaboration with sectors of our trading community direct-to examine the Kennedy round results and to expedite and recommend ways to exploit specific new exports prospects. I have already communicated, in fact, with the provincial ministers. These seminars will commence this autumn when our businessmen have had time to consider the relevance of the agreements to their individual operations.
{Mr. Winters.]
DEBATES	June 30. 1967
Over and beyond the foregoing, we in the department have commenced our own detailed study of the Kennedy round agreements to ensure that every program and activity in our trade promotion operations is tuned to maximize the realization of the new export prospects. I assure hon. members that our promotional efforts will reflect this as our prime concern. I have every expectation that Canadian businessmen will demonstrate equal resolve and effort. As recommended by the export advisory council, we intend to encourage the formation of export committees within trade associations and to use these channels and that of seminars, regionally and within annual conferences of trade and industry associations, to support our export drive.
As to operation export, which is the item to which the hon. member just referred, final data reveal that 2,144 firms actually held interviews with our trade commissioners during their seven week, highly successful, cross-Canada tour. This figure is a new record for operations of this type. This preliminary review indicates that half these firms are new to the export field or inexperienced in exporting.
The department is analysing all the data of operation export 1967. We feel sure the information derived will be useful in furthering our trade promotional activities and programs. For example, 10 per cent of the participating firms were subsidiaries of foreign parents. That indicates an increasing willingness on the part of foreign subsidiaries operating in Canada to enter the export field. Again, we will be able to identify firms by province and city of residence and degree of export experience, as a step in determining whether the concentrations of such firms warrant, say, a group approach to guidance in the techniques and practices of export. The trade commissioners who took part in the operation have now returned to their posts and are following up on the more than 16,000 interviews they held. The first progress reports on the results will be submitted before the year end.
As hon. members know, exports are only one side of the trade picture; it is a side that helps to stimulate our domestic economy, provide jobs and also helps to bring about a high level of economic performance. Imports, Mr. Chairman, are the other side and as a nation we import almost as much as we export. The importing of goods and services, and importing as an industry, all contribute to our high standard of living. Moreover, it is fair to say that we must import in order to export. Trade
June 30, 1967

is a two-way street and will be more so when the concessions of the Kennedy round are fully implemented. Canadians, I think, too often look abroad for sources of supply without first finding out if the goods and services are available in Canada. As a result, over the past five years while our exports grew to three quarters as much again as in 1961, our imports have grown almost as much.
Last year we had a substantial favourable trade balance. Unfortunately that was not quite as much as was reflected by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics year end figures. I want to inform hon. members of the discrepancy and the reason for it. It was found, in the course of confirming the earlier figures in 1967, that one important port had failed to submit its export figures to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics in time to have them included in the year end figures. The appropriate officers of the D.B.S. did not detect the discrepancy in time; as a result there was fault on both sides.
This has been reported in the press. It has been intimated that the favourable trade balance might in fact disappear. I can assure hon. members that while the trade balance might be reduced as against the figure reported by D.B.S., it will still be favourable. I can also assure hon. members that adequate steps and precautions are being taken to see that there will not be any recurrence of such a discrepancy.
There are other features of the department, very important ones, that I will not deal with at length at this time. I should refer, I think, to Expo '67 because it has received considerable attention in the world, not to mention the attention of Canadians. It has demonstrated that it is a great credit to Canada.
Hear, hear.

It will give us a new sense of national pride and status. I doubt whether Canadians ever again, after 1967, will feel that they are the kind of Canadians they were when they entered 1967. I think we shall adopt a new approach, with higher resolve, increased status and a greater pride, in ourselves and our country.
The attendance figures at Expo are striking in themselves. Yesterday, for example, a total of 267,318 guests attended, for a total to date of 16,535,419, which is considerably above the estimates. However, despite the fact that visitors are coming to Expo far in excess of expectations, the corresponding revenues have not been commensurately great. So far,
Supply-Trade and Commerce the people who have visited Expo have spent rather less per capita within the gates than had been anticipated. It is thought that when the flow of United States visitors arrives during the holiday season the slack will be taken up. It may be of interest to note that the total receipts as of June 22 from admission sales, advance admission sales and other revenues from visitors, including revenues from concessions and the performing arts, were expected to be of the order of $59 million whereas actual receipts totalled about $56 million, somewhat lower.
(12 noon)
The success of Expo will not be judged, however, from the financial returns within the gates. We always anticipated a substantial short-fall of revenues against expenditures within the gates of Expo itself. We as a government-and I know this is true of the government which preceded us-count on the financial success of Expo being reflected in its benefits across Canada and in the receipts which will accrue to the treasury through other channels.
I am sure that in the long run the net beneficial effects to Canada, financial and otherwise, will be substantial. I did want to tell hon. members of the great success of the exhibition as an attraction to visitors and point out at the same time that though revenues are not running quite as high as the number of visitors might indicate, the success of Expo is assured.

Mr. Chairman, I was interested in the statement the minister made with regard to the $100 million discrepancy. I am sure the explanation he has given will satisfy all hon. members.
I was pleased to hear the hon. gentleman repeat what he said last night with regard to the seminars which are to be held in conjunction with provincial ministers. I should like to ask whether members of parliament will be invited to attend these seminars, regardless of the party they may happen to represent. This is a subject of great interest to members of parliament.
I am sure all members will be pleased with the decision to discuss the items involved in the tariff changes next week rather than today. I believe it would be almost impossible for anyone to become conversant with this intricate subject in the very short time during which the details have been available to hon. members.

The minister was asked today whether he would agree to have this matter referred to the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. In fact, he was asked in one of the meetings of that committee on June 8, I believe, whether these tariff changes would be studied in the committee. It appears to me that the minister intended this to happen and that the members of the committee were also under that impression. This is what the minister said, according to the report of the committee's proceedings on June 8, page 40:
I would be glad to come together with you on an ad hoc basis, on a study group basis, or any other basis you wish to approach it. I think it would be a wonderful opportunity to help to disseminate information about what is going to be the most important development in the trading world in this generation.
I believe this clearly indicates that it was the intention of the minister that the whole question should be studied further by the committee. If we read further, we find mention of the fact that various firms could be invited to give evidence before the committee.
Dealing with the votes under the heading "General Administration", I believe the picture presented is somewhat misleading, though not intentionally so. The estimates are up by almost $4 million. The cost of running the standards branch is to rise by roughly $150,000. The estimate for Expo is down by $1,921,000, which is understandable because last year we were naturally spending great sums of money on this outstanding event. I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister and his department as well as all those people who were in any way responsible for the conduct of its affairs and the construction and administration of Expo '67. I am sure all hon. members who have visited Expo, as I have done, will agree with me that one's heart just naturally swells with pride over the fact that one is a Canadian, and we have such a great achievement.
Hear, hear.

I think it would be particularly remiss of me if I did not also take the opportunity to congratulate the former administration, first, for selecting the site and, second, for choosing the first committee. They were the ones who actually got the ball rolling; it was their baby, so to speak. Expo is doing a fine public relations job for our country, and I think every one of us should be proud to have even a small part in this affair.
Farther down the list of items are some which are of particular interest to me. From the entry at the bottom of page 492 we note

Grant to the Pacific National Exhibition, Vancouver. towards the cost of constructing a trade fair and sports building at Exhibition Park, Vancouver. the government of Canada's share not to exceed $2,000,000.

According to the details given on page 494 there is an increase of 15 per cent in the administrative staff. We are again back to the old empire building program in government at a time when the accent should be on saving, on cutting the estimates and saving the taxpayers' money. At present people are carrying such a fantastic tax load that they have reached the limit in this field. Now we must go to work on the other end and see where we can secure definite savings. As with all other departments, and in particular with the Department of Trade and Commerce, we shall have to work hard with the goal in mind of increasing departmental productivity.

Mr. Chairman, I would direct the attention of the committee to the list of trade posts abroad under vote 5. The total amount of the estimate for these posts has been increased somewhat, but I gather increases in rates of pay have had quite a bit to
June 30, 1967	COMMONS
do with it. We seem to have closed two offices and opened four others. I wonder why the office at Bombay was closed leaving only one in New Delhi to cover the great subcontinent of India. I notice there are two offices in Pakistan, at Islamabad and Karachi, and I think it possible there would be sufficient co-operation in that area for one of those offices to deal with matters on the west coast of India. I would be interested to know whether this is the case and whether consideration will be given to transferring one office to handle trade affairs in that vast area. It would also appear that we have no office in the great city of Calcutta.
Throughout the Pacific area our offices are few in number. We have two very close together, at Kuala Lumpur and Singapore. One wonders whether it is necessary to have two so close together, especially since the only other one in the area is at Tokyo. We are sadly unrepresented throughout the area of the Pacific rim. I would mention specifically Seoul, the capital of Korea, Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, and Taipei, the capital of Taiwan.
The Prime Minister made a special trip to British Columbia to assure the Canadian west that the government was keenly interested in Pacific trade, was doing all it could to encourage it and in fact was doing so much that the provinces were told not to bother. Yet when we examine the details of the estimates we are bound to wonder how genuine is the Prime Minister's argument and how sincere is the government in its protestations of doing all it can for Pacific trade. I would be interested to know whether there are plans to open additional trade offices in that part of the world during the coming year. It is an area which is sadly unrepresented either by diplomatic offices or trade offices. We do not have offices in several countries where we should have representation of some kind.
One of the offices which has been closed was at Salisbury and one of the new offices opened was at Nairobi. I gather that is an attempt to make up in that vast area of east Africa for under-representation of Canadian interests. It would be more correct to question on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs some of Canada's trading actions in that area, but at the moment I would be interested to know whether the office at Nairobi will be able to represent us fully in that very large and very diverse area of Africa.

Mr. Chairman, I would take advantage of this opportunity to mention a few things about the trading practices of the government in the hope that my remarks will be constructive and enlightening. I do not intend to deal with the effect of the GATT tariff cuts on Canadian industry at this time, but I do wish to point out to the minister that in my judgment Canada still marches along on a set path, showing no imagination with regard to taking advantage of the opportunities that exist for us as a nation in the field of world trade.
Most of the remarks I am going to make I made in the house three years ago and since then I have waited, relatively in vain, to see some indication that the government was going to take action on my proposals. For the interest of the new Minister of Trade and Commerce I am going to repeat in summary the ideas I put forward on October 8, 1964.
First of all, it is very clear that world trade patterns are expanding primarily among the industrial nations of the world. Over the last four years the efforts in the Kennedy round of negotiations were designed to increase this flow. It is equally obvious that the trade patterns of the newly developing nations are not developing at the rate they should. This poses a challenge to us. We in the industrial nations of the world are now faced with two major choices. One is that we should use our great and growing wealth in a combined operation of giving handouts to the newly developing nations to try to keep them afloat, and the other choice is to push self-help proposals. One of these self-help proposals is epitomized in the phrase "trade, not aid."
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The facts of life are that events since the last war indicate that nothing that has been done in the effort to bring the newly developing nations into the world trade pattern has succeeded. We are growing richer; they are growing poorer. All we are doing at the present time under the GATT concept is simply gathering the rich nations of the world into a club where we are building a high wall of tariffs around ourselves and offering a few crumbs to the poor at the door. This is moving our western world toward the first choice, the choice of handouts. This means that we stir the animosity of the individuals who live in these countries and arouse their national opposition. In the interests of Canada and in the interest of world peace I maintain that some nation in the western world must break through the wall of the rich man's club which
2156	COMMONS
Supply-Trade and Commerce we have built around our countries and do more than just hand out crumbs at the door.
What I have done before and what I intend to do now is merely outline in simple points some of the proposals that have been made and then record, as I know it, the progress which has been made in respect of them. The first proposal which I think would be accepted by all people who are knowledgeable in respect of world trading patterns is the wisdom of supporting the idea of international commodity agreements. We have had commodity agreements before and we will have them in the future. The main proposal I am making in respect of commodity agreements is one which I believe is now widely accepted by the parliamentarians in every country of the world. It is that commodity agreements should be broken into two groups, first, those dealing with the products of the newly developing nations and, second, the staple products of the industrial nations. In concerning myself first with the newly developing nations may I say that primarily they have a staple product or two to sell. Yet in our traditional bargaining practices we try to force their prices down to the lowest possible point.
We used to have, for example, a sugar agreement, but when Cuba got in trouble with the United States it collapsed. In the last year we have seen sugar prices go down to their lowest level in 35 years. This is a great advantage to many consumers in such countries as the United States and Canada but actually it is the worst thing in the world for us. We may save a cent or two a pound on our sugar, but when we buy from these newly developing nations and force them to take a low price we force them into lower and lower levels of living which only build up grief for us in the future.
I think we should deliberately send our representatives to UNCTAD this autumn with instructions to state that it is Canadian government policy, supported by all parties, that we as a nation will enter into commodity agreements with the newly developing nations so they will receive an enhanced price for their primary products and so that their producers will be given a much better chance to attain a better living standard. We on our part will voluntarily accept any greater costs which come to us in this regard. I know that such an agreement must be backed up by undertakings that those countries which accept the benefit of voluntarily higher minimum prices under the agreement will look after the question of surpluses, will see that

DEBATES	June 30, 1967
the money gets through to the people who need it, and so on. I think, however, that the nations of the world are ready to move in this direction.
What I am asking the minister to do is this. With the ground carefully cultivated for him in advance and with the parliamentarians of all the countries of the world accepting the principle, will he not lead the nations of the world by seeing that Canada takes this step publicly and openly and asks for the support of all people? I am certain that support will be forthcoming because the vast majority of the people of the United States and Canada and all the free countries of the world are interested in the type of help under which people will be helped to help themselves and under which the producers will get a fair price for their products. In this way there will be material benefit in the end for us. First of all, this must be done with the primary purpose of helping these people.
In the negotiations at GATT our negotiators had to be tough and hard in order to get such terrific reductions as 2 per cent here, a half per cent there and so on. They fought for four years. But there are a billion and a half people in the world who need a little help too. This is a new type of concept which could be promoted by Canada at this stage, and I believe it would do 500 times more good than the little bit of gain we have received from GATT. This is the type of thing I should like to hear the minister boast about. I should like to hear him boast that he had put his country into the forefront by trying to help the newly developing nations in a way that they could maintain their pride and make their own way upward in the world.
Second, under commodity agreements there must be a recognition of the fact that much of the world will depend on those of us who are the great producers of basic products such as copper. Canada, Russia, Africa and South America will have to provide a vast share of these products from their mines and forests which the world will need in the future. Surely in the interests of ourselves and in the interests of commerce it is about time we began to put into the rule of law some sort of concept not only of a fair price to the producer but also of protection for the consumers so that there is a minimum price, a maximum price, and between the two the laws of supply and demand will work. This stability of price would do a great deal for the producing countries like South America and Africa which are new countries, as well as Canada which is one of the newer countries of the world.
June 30, 1967

These countries will have to supply the bulk of this type of product.
There really is a need for an international world commodity agreement which will provide prices which are reasonable at the bottom and at the top and will allow competition between the two levels. After a five year period the two levels can then be renegotiated again. The countries of the world which are trying to build up the industrial segment of their economies prefer industrial price stability on their basic products. This would help us and it would help them.
I think I have said enough in respect of commodity agreements to make it clear that I consider this government has been a laggard in this regard. If the minister would go back over the questions I have asked in the past four years he will find that I have asked about the sugar agreement. First we were told that we had to wait until the prices were low before we could take action. Now the prices are low and still there is no action.
There must be some sort of leadership. It cannot always come from the civil service. 1 know that the Department of Trade and Commerce has a good reputation as a "go, go, go" department compared with other departments which are known as "no, no, no" departments. But everything cannot be done through the civil service. There must be leadership at the political level. There must be the kind of leadership under which we will be able to go to the various cities of Canada and say that these are ideas which we think will in the long run be in the interests of this country and certainly in the interests of world trade and the peace of the world.

The second proposal I wish to offer is in respect of the necessity today to have international trading companies. Supply-Trade and Commerce assure the minister that we support his concept. I hope, however, that the minister's mind will be flexible enough to agree that if there is a new type of institution which could be established to help this form of promotion we should support it.

As a matter of fact we have them in the grain business. I mentioned these before. There is the Argentinian company, the French company and the two American companies. These companies sell the bulk of the world's grain. They certainly can function more efficiently than the small grain companies in Canada. They can reduce the cost of selling goods that are graded and they can be stored and shipped so cheaply that the very small companies cannot compete. I should like to see, as a first step, a Canadian company go into the business of international trading, buying and selling, using modern electronic techniques for recording sales and purchases. In this way goods could be moved around the world very much cheaper than they can be moved by private companies. Through this type of international trading these companies could go into the new countries, Indonesia, China, Ghana and Nigeria, and offer to buy all the goods they have to sell under a grade standard. The third proposal I refer to as buying and selling agencies of a national type. Let me give one or two examples of what to me are lost opportunities. I have recorded figures on Hansard which indicate that in the last four years-I think it is now five-not a single dollar of Canadian money has been spent on buying rice from China. We buy $10 million worth of rice each year. China is selling rice on the world markets and is buying our wheat on the world markets; yet we in Canada do not buy one single dollar's worth of rice from China. Is this because China will not meet the grade or the price? The answers to those questions do not hold water. There are only six companies marketing rice in Canada and five of them are American. They naturally sell rice from the producing areas of Louisiana and California. They do not hunt markets for other people when they are growing this product themselves.
I say it is in Canada's interest to help the countries that are buying from us by selling their products in this country. Most of the things China produces will not sell here, but this is one product that will sell. We do not produce any rice, except a little wild rice in Manitoba and western Ontario, but we do not buy one dollar's worth of our rice from China. We buy every dollar's worth of rice from the United States. This is the result of a lack of energy on the part of private enterprise and certainly on the part of the government in getting behind private enterprise to set up some sort of group that could buy these products from companies which sell them and then make them available through regular business channels and through the big shopping centres which distribute most of the rice in Canada.
I use this as a small example of the lack of initiative on the part of this government. There are no dynamics. The government just sits still and watches things develop. I am no socialist but I think that private business to

be properly efficient should set up a type of buying agency to bring rice in of a standard grade, put it in the right type of packages and set up the selling apparatus that is apparently required to sell rice in the big shopping chains. The shopping chains themselves will do nothing. First of all, they do not believe in doing anything. They wait for the buyers to come to them. This is a laissez-faire type of operation. The buyers are only interested in goods coming from their distribution agencies. They do not care whether we buy rice from the United States or China. Let me give another example. Canada is one of the world's great producers of paper and newsprint. We now hold about 20 per cent of the world market. The world is desperate for newsprint. The reports of the FAO for 1949, 1959, and again in 1964 indicate the serious emergency we are approaching. Yet there has been no effort on the part of our newsprint industry to move into state trading areas in a big way. They only deal with the areas which can provide an enterprise type of operation. State trading nations are customers and they do not want to deal with 29 companies which handle paper; they want to deal with one.
It is about time that somebody with the force of persuasion asked our 29 paper companies in western Canada which produce newsprint to take advantage of the amendments to the Combines Investigation Act of 1959 and form a single export company to go to these state trading nations. The same thing could apply on the east coast in dealing with these new countries in Africa, for example, which have to be state trading nations for a good many decades. We need some form of buying and selling agency to bridge the gulf between our highly complicated private enterprise companies and these new countries which will be state trading countries for many years to come. This is the area in which we need dynamics and leadership. I am sure that with a little bit of push these Canadians companies are not going to resist making money for too long.

Mr. Chairman, that is a pretty full slate. I shall try to answer the questions roughly in the order in which they were asked. If I miss any I am sure the hon. member will not mind refreshing my memory, as I did not make a note of his questions seriatim.
I think he referred first to the Hong Kong office and to the increase of approximately $53,000 in the estimate. He will note that we added two officers to the office. We also obtained new office premises which involved us in the acquisition of more space at higher cost. That office has become quite a centre of operations because most of our negotiations with China are through Hong Kong. We have no access to mainland China at the present time. Our main item of trade with China is wheat, which they are taking on time and paying for on schedule. Our wheat contracts are in good shape.
It is hard to be precise in answering what our trading policy is with that country to which we have no direct access in the geographic sense. They come to Hong Kong and we go to Hong Kong, which is not a good arrangement, but the trade we do apart from wheat is not very great. We are hoping that our trade will become greater. We are also hoping that the opportunity to sell more wheat to China will continue. We shall probably do so through Hong Kong, though certainly if we could open a direct channel to Peking-I hope we can do so very soon because

Supply-Trade and Commerce our present way of doing business is frustrating-it would be most beneficial.
I think the hon. member asked next a question about sugar.
Yes.

The hon. member asked about an international sugar agreement. The hon. member may recall from my previous statements that we are pressing for an international sugar agreement. This would be one way to benefit the lesser developed countries which are so reliant on sugar to support their economies. We have stated to the British commonwealth countries of the West Indies that we would make available to them the residual amount of tariffs under the preferential tariff structure, which would mean about 29 cents a hundredweight in respect of sugar that they sell us this year, up to a total amount-I have forgotten the exact figure but I think it is for 275,000 tons. This should be helpful, but we think the long-term solution lies in a world sugar agreement. We have proposed this and we understand that Dr. Prebisch who is responsible for broader collective commodity agreements such as this will visit us this fall and we hope to advance the cause of a world sugar agreement.

What is next on the list?
Textiles, nickel and copper.

As to textiles, the hon. member has probably had an opportunity to read the material I tabled last night concerning the Kennedy round concessions made by Canada as against the access gained by Canada to other countries, and I think he will recognize that here too we have been able to minimize the impact of the Kennedy round concessions on the textile industry. Perhaps I should refer to a note I have on my desk to the effect that Dr. Prebisch, the director general of UNCTAD, expects to visit a number of capitals to discuss the possibility of new international agreements this year, and he will probably visit Ottawa. On the subject of nickel, this commodity is still in short supply. This program is working reasonably well, even though it means that the companies have not been able to serve their foreign markets as well as they would like because they are giving some measure of preference to domestic requirements.

I mentioned the export trade bank.

I presume the hon. member is referring to the Export Credit Insurance Corporation which insures exports and also reimburses banks on a non-recourse basis. We finance exports by private companies as part of a program which has played a significant role in increasing our exports abroad.
I have asked the officials of the corporation to generate ideas for improving the application of export insurance to Canadian exports and I have asked the advisory council whether they have any ideas on the subject. 1 have also asked members of the banking fraternity if they can generate ways and means, within the structure of the banks themselves, of providing better support facilities for Canadian exports. While I believe the present arrangements are working well, there is always room for improvement and I am trying to find ways and means of bringing improvement about.

I appreciate the answers the minister has given me. Only this morning I happened to read an article in which the need for greater effort in this particular field of participation in our export endeavours was indicated. I appreciate the active consideration which the minister is giving to this problem.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak for very long. I realize that as a result of the agreement which was made this morning I am prevented from dealing in detail with results of the Kennedy round. As a


matter of fact, quite apart from the agreement which was reached, anyone examining the material which was made available will understand that the sheer bulk of this information would prevent any intelligent discussion now. However, under this item I am able to deal with trade in general and the benefits which flow to this country from the use of our trade commissioners.
I am all in favour of the minister's view, as he expressed it in reply to my hon. friend from Wellington South, that this service is not a frill but a hardworking agency essential to our economic development and to trade relations between Canada and countries abroad. I might even suggest to the minister that from time to time trade commissioners who have returned to this country should be asked to appear before the standing committee to give hon. members some indication of the success they have had in their work and what they hope to achieve in the future. I do not propose that this be done wholesale, as it were, but occasionally it would be of benefit to all concerned if members were given an opportunity to examine some of these commissioners and listen to their views.
I stand here as an unrepentant, unrestricted and, at times, very isolated believer in the greatest possible measure of free trade. I am still optimistic, even after being here for more than nine years. This, of course, means complete free trade, and to achieve complete free trade is almost as difficult as it is for politicians, particularly privy councillors, to reach heaven. Nevertheless, what we have achieved so far is very substantial. I only wish we could have done more.
I am one who believes it was unfortunate that the United Kingdom did not enter the European Common Market early enough to take advantage of the provision in the United States trade expansion act under which a 100 per cent tariff reduction might have come into effect with results even more far reaching in the future than those which have now been achieved. When the treaty of Rome became effective we saw the freer movement of labour, capital and goods within the four corners of the E.C.M., the tremendous expansion of trade which occurred, the development of industry and commercial activity, the general increase in the standard of living in the countries concerned, and surely these are the best arguments anyone could use as to the benefits which flow from freedom to trade and exchange goods and services among all parts of the world.

One of the reasons for the levelling off, at least, of trade and industrial activity within the common market nations today is that having reached a substantial degree of trade expansion they now find themselves restricted as a trading market by the common tariff barrier they have erected against other nations and trading blocs in the world. In any event this is my view, and I think it is one held by many other people. I have no hesitation in expressing my satisfaction that we have been able to go as far as we have. I understand it is not unlikely that further legislation will be sought by the executive of the United States from congress. I assume the minister will be kept posted as to the extent of such legislation and I hope it will be matched by the efforts which we make on our side. This is particularly essential considering the position of the undeveloped nations.

I know this is trite. I know these cliches are used over and over again by people in public life not only in Canada but in other parts of the world. But cliches are clichds because they are statements and restatements of facts, of what is obvious, and they are uttered every so often as evidence of the truthfulness of the facts contained in the statements.
At present some 25 or 26 nations of the world which have the lowest per capita income have the highest rate of population growth. Conversely 30 nations with the highest per capita income have the lowest rate of population growth. The effect of this is very simple. Inside a comparatively short period of time, instead of half of the world being hungry, three quarters of the world is going to be very hungry. Nations are like people, and when that happens they are going to look about and seek ways and means of taking what they have been deprived of. We as one of the great trading nations, as one of the developed nations, must play our part through the aid of the trade commissioners' offices and all the other various weapons which we can place at the command of the government.
Much is being done in the furnishing of aid by Canada and other countries. Not so many years ago I noted that even if we took all of the aid in the form of capital goods, loans, cash, and the dispatch of trained people with certain expertise and knowledge to assist in the development of the underprivileged nations, and added to that the actual dollars or sterling earned by them through the sale of their products, there would still be an enormous gap amounting to $10 billion or $12

Supply-Trade and Commerce billion between what they were earning and what was being given to them and what they required to produce in their own country the plant and the capital goods they need to make their standard of living a reasonable one.
Because of this the developed nations should stretch a point wherever possible to take from those countries, even at some sacrifice to us from time to time, a greater measure of their products than normally might be the case, especially from countries with whom we can develop suitable trading arrangements. In other words, it is not adequate to continue developing solely a system of aid. These underdeveloped countries must lift themselves up, so far as possible, by their own efforts. Only in this way will what we seek be gained. In our trade relations with developing nations we should seek from time to time to accept from them, at a lower tariff rate than would normally be the case, goods which we can use in Canada and thereby provide additional capital to assist those nations.
That is all I propose to say, Mr. Chairman. I wanted to make my position clear because I probably will not be here during the latter part of next week when this issue is to be debated. My views are very strong. I have held them with conviction for a long time. I only regret that during my years in this chamber there has not been one example of an intelligent discussion and debate on the question of foreign aid. We have touched on it concurrently and incidentally when dealing with other matters. I believe that on an issue so important to Canada it is important that we debate it in the house and in committee.
One of the reasons that we will be entering into discussion of the Kennedy round of negotiations is that there has been a great deal of apprehension about the outcome. I recall two or three years ago asking the minister's predecessor to consider producing a white paper which, without harming the efforts of our negotiating officials at Geneva, would give an indication of the government's views and intentions so that we could have an intelligent debate in the house and arouse national interest in the issue. That did not happen, but from now on I hope this is a matter we will pursue more diligently.
With the assistance of the minister and the use of committees we can achieve a greater consciousness of our trade relations with other countries, of the trade agreements which have been made and the trade agreements which are being contemplated. This is only a

I am sorry I cannot give a breakdown but I suspect we have been receiving more local visitors in proportion to the total than was anticipated. I would guess from the level of expenditure that Montrealers in particular have been patronizing Expo in a very great way which, of course, is right and proper. We anticipate that the proportion of foreign visitors, particularly from the United States, will increase substantially now that the schools are closed and families can travel with their children to Expo.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)

This brings me to the point I would like to make. I suspect that the overflow of visitors is mainly due to the fact that Canadians have taken Expo to heart, particularly, as the minister mentioned, the local people within a radius of approximately 100 miles of Montreal. They have gone all out to visit Expo and have reacted with great enthusiasm to what they have seen and experienced. I think it is worth while to note that the vast majority of these people are French speaking Canadians. When questioning local people on the grounds it is not uncommon to hear them say that they have visited Expo eight, 10, 12 or even 14 times. If there is any lesson in respect of unity and pride which can be taken from Expo I think it is the overwhelmingly enthusiastic interest which has been shown by the people within this radius of Montreal.
The lessons to be derived certainly are far reaching. It is worth noting that in a small city like Lachute at least 90 per cent of the school children above grade four have visited Expo where they have had a great lesson in Canadian pride and the potential of Canadian accomplishment. I believe it is true that one cannot visit Expo without leaving it a little bit more Canadian. I think it is worth

while to note that French speaking Canadians have gone all out for this all-Canadian venture. I believe that out of it will develop a great degree of Canadian pride from coast to coast. I believe it will provide a great contribution toward an all-Canadian unity. I believe it is more than likely that this will be the main byproduct of Expo.
It is particularly important that this be underlined at this time because in past months we have read on occasion certain statements which have been made by radicals in all quarters. These people who speak of separatism and independence unfortunately receive much coverage in the news media across the country. I believe we should take this opportunity to underline that these people who often try to put forward the idea that they are speaking on behalf of French Canadians have no mandate and no authority to speak in that manner.
When speaking to various groups across Canada in past years I have had the opportunity to say that my name is Roger Regimbal, my constituency is Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes and that I come from "la belle province de Quebec". I say that I am French but reasonable. The essential footnote to add to that, however, is that there are millions like me in the province of Quebec but unfortunately they do not get headlines. Therefore we should take an opportunity like this to underline for the benefit of all Canadians that French Canadians are aboard, are very much a part of this enterprise, and wish to be identified as being a part of it.
I believe that the enthusiastic response to Expo by Quebeckers, old and young, is without doubt an indication, contrary to the impression which might be given by the outlandish statements made by certain individuals, that when the chips are down and it is time to act and show solidarity and pride in Canada, French Canadians like other Canadians, no matter in what domain, whether it be industry, commerce, or finance, will deliver the goods.
I should like to say that I believe the hon. member deserves a great many headlines today.

say to him that there are some people from western Canada who sometimes create a bad impression of that wonderful land.
These words have to be spoken. I hope they get the attention they deserve. I did not rise to speak on this subject, Mr. Chairman, but I was interested in what my colleague said. I express my regret that the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce have reached the House of Commons just at a time when the attention of so many people is engaged elsewhere because of the royal visit. This is a department which deserves great attention from the House of Commons because of its importance to our economy and because of the good work that the trade commissioners have been doing over the years in so many posts abroad. I should like every year, when the opportunity arises, to pay my tribute to the work done by the people in the department and particularly by the trade commissioners with whom I had a very pleasant experience during a relatively short interval.
I know of no department that is of greater interest. I know of no department that is more efficient than the Department of Trade and Commerce. I do not believe there is any department which does more abroad for Canada than it does. I do not wish to appear to be downgrading the Department of External Affairs which also works abroad, but the expansion of our trade has always seemed to me to be more important than some of our activities in diplomatic circles. Supply-Trade and Commerce came about as a result of the activity to which I have raised objections on other occasions, namely, the imposition of sanctions against Rhodesia. I have expressed the hope that now it has become evident that the imposition of economic sanctions against that country has not been effective in achieving the objectives that were set out at the commonwealth conference, steps will be taken to remove those sanctions and re-open trade with Rhodesia.
When this matter was discussed earlier in the House of Commons and the sanctions were imposed the impression was left with us that within a matter of a few months they would be effective and that the political settlement desired by some of the leaders of the commonwealth would be achieved. That has not been the case. I hope the minister will use his good influence to see that there is a lifting of these economic sanctions in order that we may once again establish a trade mission in Rhodesia and resume trade with that country.
We trade with virtually all the countries of the world. We have grave differences with some of them in respect of political matters but we have not hesitated to engage in trade with communist countries with which we are frequently not in agreement. We continue to trade with various countries which have suffered a number of coups d'etat. Their governments have been upset and unitary governments or military dictatorships have been established. We have continued to trade with them but we have cut ourselves off from trading relations with Rhodesia. It is a country which has not been subject to military dictatorship or any serious internal trouble but which has had a political difference of opinion with Great Britain.
For 43 years Rhodesia had the right to act independently in respect of all matters except defence and foreign policy. Yet Canada at the urging of various people immediately swung into line and severed relations with Rhodesia. I think that diplomatic relations should be resumed and that trade relations should also be resumed. Why should we continue to trade with certain other countries which have effected bloody revolutions and where the heads of state have been assassinated or disposed of in one way or another and not trade with Rhodesia? Canada's response in many of these instances has been an immediate recognition of the new government. Yet in respect of Rhodesia we broke off relations and imposed economic sanctions. This is a blot on our record.

We have heard on many occasions that one way toward maintaining peace in the world is through friendly trading relations. Yet with this country of the commonwealth we have broken off trading relations and set up a barrier. We can afford to have a difference of opinion in respect of how the government of Rhodesia should operate but surely this should not extend to the realm of our trading relations. Can we not maintain our trading relations with Rhodesia despite our difference of opinion in respect of political matters? We continue our trading relations with Nigeria which appears to be on the verge of a civil war. We are entering into and have carried on trade with nations in Europe which are under Russian domination. We have not hesitated to trade with Russia, although we have never approved of its form of government. So it goes all down the line, even with the African country of Ghana, the government of which was upset and the premier expelled. We immediately recognized the new government and continued our trading relations. We have maintained our trade post there. I ask this question of a minister of the crown who in our opinion on this side of the house ranks as being one of the more reasonable members of the treasury benches.

In 1966-67 the Minister of National Revenue used a sleight-of-hand procedure and extracted money from the contingency fund and from other sources in order to avoid the difficulty which he was having over the voting of interim supply. I do not know whether the 1966-67 figure means that the department paid back to the contingency fund $761,700. That may be all right for 1966-67, but why should there be over $1 million in the unallocated and miscellaneous fund for 1967-68? The minister does not have to go through the same procedure as the Minister of National Revenue did.

The reason for unexpended moneys is to be found, for example, in the office in Salisbury for which we budgeted but
June 30. 1967

which was not opened. We had some unexpended funds in Havana and in Belgrade where the office was not opened as early as was anticipated. There were some unexpended funds in Colombo, Geneva, the United Nations office in New York and all other embassies where we do not have representation where minor expenses were incurred by the Department of External Affairs on a recoverable basis. The sum total adds up to the figure indicated.
I do not know what the Auditor General will think of this but I do not think much of an unallocated sum of $1 million.
It is better than to have an over-expenditure of $1 million.

The minister is expected to be specific in requesting supply from the House of Commons and to give us the specific items. This has been done all the way through vote No. 5 up to this item. I would not call it a slush fund but some people who are not as careful in their use of language as I am might do so. I can see the minister is anticipating the employment of 22 more people for whom provision must be made. This would come under "miscellaneous". It seems to me that $266,765 is adequate for the office in Paris where 22 or 23 people are employed, but here we have an unallocated sum of $1 million. If it were not for the fact that we are here on a Friday afternoon when all sorts of interesting activities are going on in town I would move to have that sum reduced to $1.
I gave the minister a few seconds in order to devise a better and more palatable explanation of this unspecified appropriation of funds. The minister says it is better to have it this way than to overspend, but the practice of bringing in supplementary estimates has been well established and when a department overspends, makes a mistake or has to enlarge its activities, supplementary estimates are brought in to cover the amount of money that is expended. However, the Minister of Trade and Commerce is expansively asking for a blank cheque for $1 million. I do not want to be too hard on him because he agreed with me with regard to Rhodesia, which is good.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Did the minister agree with the hon. member?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: In that case I withdraw what I said about him.

The hon. member was an exponent of a one man, one vote policy in Rhodesia with which I disagree completely. I do not want to be too hard on the minister, but I wonder whether he has a better explanation for this unallocated sum.

The only supplementary information I can give is that out of the total amount of $1 million, $687,150 relates to funds provided for retroactive salary revisions which were allocated from the financial contingency fund. These were not prorated to individual offices. It was set up in this way at the request of the Treasury Board.
Should it not have been set up separately as it was in 1966-67?

Perhaps it should; I am not sure. I do not know the precise reason for that. The only reason I know for doing it this way is that it was done at the request of the Treasury Board and I understand it carries the judgment of the Auditor General.

Item agreed to.
10. Canadian Government Exhibition Commission, $5,258,000.

Mr. Chairman, let us not rush through this item. As I said earlier today, we are not under any obligation to pass the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce under a guillotine procedure, as we are with regard to four other departments. These estimates may very well be concluded later. I think we should be a little careful about rushing things through today and voting money without obtaining an adequate explanation.
However, this is not my only reason for rising at this point. The Canadian Government Exhibition Commission is a very active branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce and it does not always receive the recognition it deserves. There are 125 people working in that branch and they are continually on the job preparing government exhibitions in various places around the world. I think that the minister, who takes some pride in his work, would not mind at this stage taking a few minutes to tell us what this commission is doing and what, for example, it has done over the last year as well as what are its plans for the future. In the course of his remarks he might tell us whether they are already starting on work for the world's fair which will be held in Tokyo. The
June 30, 1967

Supply-Trade and Commerce Canadian Government Exhibition Commission is too important a section of the Department of Trade and Commerce to pass without attention. It is a very worth-while commission and the public should be informed through the House of Commons, and for the sake of the members as well, just what the commission is doing, e (2:20 p.m.)

I agree, Mr. Chairman, that this is an important part of the departmental function and it is a very good operation in my opinion. The commission is responsible for setting up Canadian exhibits around the world when we participate in fairs. I believe it does a highly creditable job. It was responsible, among other things, for setting up the display in the caravans that are operating under the general jurisdiction of the Secretary of State. I had an opportunity to see one of these caravans and was extremely impressed by it.
There is a great list of fairs and shows around the world in which Canada participates. One recent example was the air show in Paris where the department set up the exhibit and helped to service it. This air show was attended by my colleague, the Minister of Transport. Perhaps he could give his own opinion on whether or not the exhibit was suitable.
Why didn't you go instead?

The Minister of Transport has more direct responsibility for aviation than I have, and it was an air show. There is a long list of fairs in which we participate but I am sure the hon. member would not want me to mention them.
Would the minister mention half a dozen of the more important ones?

Yes. For example, we are participating in the Alaska centennial celebrations in Alaska, which will take place from May 27 to September 1, 1967; the international exposition for 1988 which is known as the hemisfair, in San Antonio, Texas; the Japan world exposition, which is known as Expo '70 and is scheduled to be held in Osaka in 1970. The Canadian government has agreed to spend there an estimated amount of $11.2 million.
We held a competition to which we had a response from over 200 architects and architectural firms. The 200 entries were narrowed down to six finalists from which we selected a design which was unveiled just last


week. The winning firm of architects is a well known firm from Vancouver by the name of Erickson-Massey. I believe the design they have produced is highly imaginative and will attract considerable attention. Our participation in Osaka will cost $11.2 million, including everything, but the building itself will cost very much less than that.
This is a creative branch of the department, and I think the work done in this field is in keeping with that done by any other country in the world. If the hon. member would like me to give details on what we have done or what we will be doing, I will be glad to give them.

I think it is very important that there should be a more detailed list given. I realize the list is given in the annual report. However, an opportunity is presented here to attract the attention of members who might not, because of pressure of work, read the annual report. There is an opportunity, despite the press releases issued by the minister's office, to draw the attention of the news media to this branch. I presume there are business enterprises in Canada that sometimes do not take full advantage of the opportunities provided by these exhibits. The minister might also tell us what part, if any, this branch played at Expo '67 in Montreal.

At Expo '67 in Montreal the trade fair people played a prominent role in laying out the exhibit in the Canadian pavilion and they were consulted widely with regard to other layouts. I feel that as a result the Canadian pavilion is a very good place. I have a long list of fairs in which the Canadian government is participating. I could give a few examples. In January there was the SAE Automotive Engineering Congress and Exhibition in Detroit; the National Boat Show in New York; the International Hardware Trades Fair in London. In February there was the National Sporting Goods Association Convention at Chicago. In March there was the Boston Gift Show, Boston; the Salon International de l'Agriculture, Paris; the Netherlands Industries Fair, Utrecht; Daily Mail Ideal Home Exhibition, London; Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers Conference and Exhibition in New York and the Canadian Housing Exhibit, Paris. In April there was the International Children's and Babies Fair, Cologne; the American Society for Tool and Manufacturing Engineers Exhibition, Chicago; the International Engineering Exhibition, London and the International Fur Fair, Frankfurt. In May there
June 30, 1967

was the American Institute of Architects Convention, New York and the Salon International de l'Aeronautique et l'Espace, Paris. In June, there was the Barcelona International Samples Fair, Barcelona; the Supermarket Institute Show, Cleveland; the 36th Poznan International Fair, Poznan, and so on. Do you wish me to read the others?
Go on, that is very good.

In August we will be participating in the New York Gift Show, New York; the Belfast Telegraph Ideal Home Show, Belfast. In September, there is the International Autumn Fair, Zagreb, where I had the pleasure of visiting last year, and the International Trade Fair, Brno, where I also had the pleasure of visiting. There is the National Office Furniture and Equipment Show, Chicago, the International Exhibition of Fine Foods and Provisions, Cologne and the International Dairy Cattle Fair at Cremona.
In October, Mr. Chairman, there is the German Industries Fair, Berlin; the National Shoe Fair of America, Chicago; the Salon Technique International de l'Equipement Hotelier du Materiel de Cafeteria et des Industries Connexes, which is an exhibition of hotel, cafeteria and catering equipment in case hon. members did not understand my brand of French. This will take place in Paris. Then there is the American Society for Metals Show, Cleveland; Electra '67, Johannesburg; the International Fair for Sports Goods, Camping Equipment and Garden Furniture, Cologne; Pacific International Trade Fair, Lima. In November, there is the International Building Exhibition, London; Salon International du Batiment, Paris.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
