please. House again in committee of supply, estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, Vote No. 10. Shall vote 10 carry?

Item agreed to.
15. Canadian Government Travel Bureau-To assist in promoting the tourist business in Canada including a grant of S55.000 to the Canadian Tourist Association, $9,991,000.

One minute, Mr. Chairman. I do not want to delay matters but we have about 50 minutes at our disposal and we are dealing with a department of considerable interest. The minister himself is anxious to give a great deal of publicity to his operations in this department, and I want to help him.
Thank you.
I was associated with this department for a number of years and I know how valuable it is to Canada.
Hear, hear.

Yes. Many ministers on the government side have had some association with that department. It deserves attention. Though I do not advocate that the minister should beat the drum all the time, nevertheless I want him to draw to the attention of the House of Commons the advantages that this department brings to Canada as a whole and how the Canadian Government Travel Bureau assists in promoting the tourist business in Canada.
This item ought not to be passed without comment. Here is an opportunity for the minister once again to emphasize the value of the tourist business and of the government travel bureau. He can give us information about what the bureau has been doing under his stewardship. I assume that, as other ministers of trade and commerce have our present minister has taken some interest in this aspect of his department and is prepared to tell the committee what is going on, what his forecast of future operations is and if there is to be an expansion of this service.
Because of a number of elections and the postponement of the study of estimates, as well as other, similar considerations, we have not had a chance during the last three years to pay the same attention to departmental activities that we have paid in the past. As I said before, we suspended today's session
2176
June 30. 1967

Supply-Trade and Commerce For understandable reasons we are working under a slight disadvantage today and cannot give to this department all the attention it deserves. Nevertheless I shall ask the minister to inform us about some matters and to put on the record what this travel bureau does, how effectively it is working, what its future prospects are, as well as letting us know whether he has any suggestions toward improving the service, if it needs to be improved. He can say whether he wants the support of the members of the House of Commons in his activities, in that regard.
Sometimes ministers of the crown find that their colleagues in cabinet cause them the greatest difficulty. If they can go to a cabinet meeting and say, "The House of Commons is in favour of this proposal," that strengthens their hand in cabinet. Then there is that awful establishment called Treasury Board which rides roughshod over members of the cabinet who are not on the Treasury Board committee. I shall not recount again, as I have in the past, my experiences with Treasury Board a few years ago; but I still bear the scars. Perhaps the present minister has a different approach to Treasury Board. Maybe he is on Treasury Board himself.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

I rise on a question of privilege, as one who was a member of Treasury Board at the time to which my hon. friend is referring. He seemed to imply that ministers who were members of Treasury Board found their requests for funds dealt with much more rapidly than those who were not. I take exception to that statement.

Well, in that case, I have been under a misapprehension for a number of years, obviously. Of course I am bound to accept the statement of an hon. member made here in the House of Commons. It is my good fortune to meet this hon. member frequently in private, however, and we shall discuss this matter privately on some occasion and not burden the committee with it.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman will permit me to ask him a question before he goes on to another point. Does the exchange we have just heard indicate that he and the hon. member for Perth are now joining in the leadership race?
Well, I already have a mover and a seconder, but neither of them has as yet committed himself to vote for me.
Oh, oh.

I see no obstacle in the way of any member of this party putting his name up for leadership. As a matter of fact-this is just an aside, Mr. Chairman-I was talking to the leader of the New Democratic Party last night and I asked him how they managed things in his party. He informed me that according to their constitution there will be a vacancy as of Monday. I said: "Then you will be relieved of all your responsibility." He agreed. The burden would then be carried by the joint co-chairmen of the convention. I asked him what he would do if some statement were made of national or international importance. "Oh," he said, "I would carry on as house leader and, in that capacity, I would deal with the statement."

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Order.

I expressed the hope that the hon. gentleman would be re-elected, you know; his party can go on making mistakes if it wishes. I said I was not certain he would encounter any opposition, but I had discovered there was a surplus of candidates in the Conservative party, and we might supply some assistance in that way. His suggestion, in return, was that we might work out a lend lease program which would be of benefit to both parties.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I hate to interrupt the hon. gentleman. If he had included the words "trade and commerce" in the remarks he has just made, they would not have been out of order.
Oh, oh.
Well, Mr. Chairman, a lend lease program is, in effect, a trade exchange, and that is what I was coming to. I do not know how this interruption occurred.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: It was caused by a colleague of yours on the front bench.

No, it was an interruption by the Minister of Transport, who is frequently irrelevant. I was talking about the Canadian Government Travel Bureau, and I will now sit down and let the minister answer my questions by giving us a short resume of the activities of this bureau.
If he wants support from the committee with regard to these activities, then provided he can indicate to us that he has a knowledge of the subject we shall endeavour to support him; and this, in turn, may have a persuasive effect on his cabinet colleagues and on
June 30, 1967

Treasury Board-and it was because I mentioned Treasury Board that a sensitive member of this house rose and made some objection.

I will try to meet the rigid standard of acceptance put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. I have a long association with this operation dating back, now, to 1948 when I assumed responsibility for the Canadian Government Travel Bureau.
It has vastly improved since then.

It was then part of the department of reconstruction and supply operated under the direction of Mr. D. Leo Dolan, who had a great maritime background and heritage which he acquired largely, I think, through his association with Senator William Dennis who first sponsored what was to become the Canadian travel bureau.
We went through the pangs of building up this operation for which I was responsible until 1953, at which time it was passed to my successor, who was the Hon. Jean Lesage. I greatly enjoyed my association with the Canadian travel bureau which was then in its infancy. I officiated at the opening of its first office in the United States, in New York. We thought it was a great step forward and we wondered whether or not we could stand the expenditure. It turned out to be a good investment. This is now being followed up, and I think today we have some 23 offices abroad and are on the point of opening several others. The budget of the bureau used to be relatively modest. It is something of an experience to realize that we are now spending $10 million a year on tourist activity. Translate this in terms of results, the amount which derives from this investment of money, and the figure is just as startling-perhaps even more so. Last year, total gross revenue on this account, as far as it can be estimated-and there are no precise yardsticks-was of the order of $840 million, which was a record.
Even so, Canada experienced a net deficit on travel account, showing that Canadians are the greatest travellers in the world. On a per capita basis I think Canadian tourists spend more money than any other tourists. This may be attributable to the fact that we live in such close proximity to the great and friendly United States, and its vast opportunities for travel and purchasing.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
This year we are aiming at a total gross revenue of more than $1 billion. This will be a landmark of achievement and I think we will reach the target. If we do, we can forecast with some confidence that Canada will have a net favourable balance on travel account for the first time in our history, as far as I know.
An important development is the number of inquiries which are being generated by these 23 offices of ours around the world. I participated this year in the opening of an office in Paris. We opened another in Seattle a few days ago, and my hon. friend from Peel officiated on my behalf. During the year 1966 there were 1,808,000 inquiries, and these are now all handled by computerized devices.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
It is a marvel of modem ingenuity to see the way these inquiries are processed, replied to expeditiously, kits of material made up, all mechanically sorted, put in envelopes and dispatched. That was an all time record, more than the number of inquiries received by any other travel bureau in the world. But in the five month period this year from January through May we had the astonishing number of 2,350,000 inquiries received, thereby setting an all time record of inquiries, and giving an indication that this is going to be the greatest travel year in Canada's history. A great deal of the interest is owed to Expo '67 and all our other centennial celebrations.
And the Pan-Am games in Winnipeg.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I hope to have the privilege of attending them, and I expect to see my hon. friend at them, perhaps in the 100 yard dash.
I do not know, Mr. Chairman, how much more I have to say to qualify for approval of these estimates, but perhaps what I have said is an indication of my interest in this great government operation.

Item agreed to.
Standards branch-
20. Administration and operation, $4,323,200.

The minister has expressed great hope that as a result of the Kennedy round negotiations there will be a tremendous opportunity for Canadian manufacturing generally to find new markets throughout the world. This brings me to the fact that most of the world in which our manufacturers will find markets for their goods is already on the metric system. This trend will continue because the metric system
June 30, 1967

Supply-Trade and Commerce has tremendous benefits from the point of view of being practical. Of course it is used universally in science. It would be a great benefit if it were applied to engineering and manufacturing because it would simplify standards, right down to such things as thread measurements, sizes of buildings, manufacturing stock, etc.
The money under this vote is for the standards branch, a branch of government that operates very unobtrusively. The average person tends to forget that it exists at all, and I think it is a criterion of good government when people are not continuously aware of a branch of government because of the irritations it causes. Over the years the standards branch has been doing an excellent job. Standards are the very basis for trade. Historically, standards were the first thing that had to be established for exchange and trade.
I confine my remarks at this time to recommending that the government expedite as much as possible the study, and perhaps development on a gradual basis, of the metric system and its application to our manufacturing concerns, so that they will have the opportunity and the capability of competing with Common Market countries in the markets which the minister hopes will be opened to a greater extent to Canadian industry. I would appreciate it if the minister would bring the committee up to date on the government's thinking in this field, on what has been done, and on what is contemplated will be done toward this objective.

Of course, Mr. Chairman, we must guide ourselves by developments in the markets of the world. Our biggest market is the United States, which is still on the current standards system of inches, feet, and so on. However, I believe the trend around the world is toward the metric system. The British have indicated their readiness to adopt it, and I think have given themselves a period of some five years to phase into its adoption.
Certain segments of our economy have already come into the metric system, notablj' the photographic industry and the pharmaceutical industry. We are keeping very closely attuned to these developments, and as markets in the world develop an acceptability of the merits of the metric system we will go along with them. I do not think I can go beyond that at the moment.

Mr. Chairman, I believe it is the standards branch which is responsible for enforcing the Gas Inspection Act, the Electricity


Inspection Act and the Weights and Measures Act. These respective statutes stipulate that the fees are to be regulated so that they will cover the actual costs of inspection, but from the latest figures available to me it appears that the branch lost $735,000 on its operations in 1966. That is not the actual cost. If all the costs involved were charged to the department the loss would have been over $1 million. Why does the minister not follow the statutes in this respect, and thereby wipe out this deficit? This is something which should be watched more carefully, in view of the fact that the estimates for the whole department shows a loss of $1,672,400.
The staff of the whole branch has been increased by nine, and there is an increase of $10,000 for office supplies. The increase for travel is $31,000, yet no effort is made to have the branch pay its own way. Is consideration being given to a reassessment of fees so that it will not continue to show a loss on its operations?
This branch is also responsible for checking all measuring devices. I refer in particular to odometers, which are those parts of speedometers that register mileage travelled. I understand that nearly all speedometers imported into Canada come from the United States, and about a year ago it was stated that these speedometers, when tested, were consistently found to be 3.5 per cent over-rated. In other words they were not giving the true picture so far as mileage was concerned.
This has a direct bearing on the car rental business. People who rent cars would like to know they are paying for the actual miles they travel. People who keep close tab on gas mileage, and oil and tire performance, also want to know they are getting the true picture. Are checks being made on these speedometers which are put in Canadian cars?

Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for Wellington South for his intervention and I congratulate him on the homework he has done on this branch, which normally remains in the background but which does such valuable work in checking the system of weights and measures we have in Canada.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
For some time, I think perhaps dating back to the reign of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, we have had in mind doing something about this branch by way of broader legislative authority in order to bring it up to date. The legislative program of this
June 30, 1967

house in respect of items which have high priority has been so heavy that we have been unable to deal with this, but it is our intention as soon as possible to bring before the house legislation which will revise some aspects of the statute. We do not need to do this in order to charge fees which are more in line with the expenditures. We are looking into this matter and perhaps I will have more to say on this at a later date.

Item agreed to.
2.9. Canadian Government participation in the 1967 World Exhibition, Montreal, $6,750,800.

This vote I imagine is acceptable to the house because of the general interest in the world exhibition in Montreal and because of the general success of that enterprise. I wonder whether the minister at this stage might review this from the beginning. In addition to the estimate which appears here, perhaps he would indicate the total amount of money we have voted over the years in respect of Expo '67. In so far as he has the information, he might also give us the figures for attendance at the fair and the forecast with regard to the financial success of the exhibition.
The reason I ask for this is that although a tremendous amount of information appears in the daily press, radio and television, nevertheless I think it should be recorded in Hansard at this particular stage so that the progress to date will be included in our permanent records. This will all come out later, of course, when the world fair is over and the totals are added up, but I think an interim report at this stage would be helpful.
It is very appropriate that this should come under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is interesting to note that two very active and major figures on the staff of Expo '67-without in any way detracting from the work which has been done by others -are former members of the Department of Trade and Commerce. This is an indication of the type of able people who are employed by that department. They have had an opportunity at an international exhibition to show to everyone that we have in Canada men who are fit and capable to do things at an international exhibition which are comparable in standard to what has been done by people of other nationalities at other world exhibitions. There may be others, but I am referring to Mr. Andy Kniewasser and Mr. Leslie Brown, both of whom were very active and capable members of the Department of Trade and
Supply-Trade and Commerce Commerce when I had the pleasure and honour to report to parliament for that department.
The engineer who was largely responsible for the construction of the site and for the general arrangements surely must be, somewhere along the line, a relative of mine. I have not quite discovered the close connection, but he appears to exhibit the characteristics of the Anglo-Saxon clan to which I belong.
Although I have not said anything in the house about Expo '67 from the time of its origin, I think this is one of the great accomplishments of Canada. I had the pleasure of attending the world fair in New York in 1939, and had an excellent opportunity to see that fair in detail. I also had an opportunity to see the world fair in Brussels in 1958. Therefore I have had an opportunity to make a comparison. In so far as my recollection is concerned, those two world fairs, important as they were, have been exceeded by the extent of, and the emphasis placed upon Expo '67. Time of course has moved on and technological improvements have occurred. Nevertheless, the world fair in Canada this year, in Montreal, has set a standard which will be hard to match in the future, not only from the standpoint of the number of countries which have participated in the fair-this is a major achievement and one which I am sure must be an all time record-but also from the standpoint of the standard of competence which has been displayed at the fair.
As Canadians we naturally are very proud of having such a successful exhibition in our country. We are fully cognizant of the fact that this has attracted world attention to Canada and will result in better relations between Canada and other countries. It will also stimulate trade. We are grateful to the countries which have undertaken to participate in the fair. Thanks to a great many people-the director general whose career in external affairs is well known to the members of the house, and the competent staff -Canadians have found that in this centennial year we have been able to put on display to the world a fair which surpasses any previous world fair. I am sure we are all grateful to those who have done the planning, who have worked hard and who have participated. We are also grateful to the members of the Department of Trade and Commerce for their contribution.
So, at this stage I should like to ask the minister to give us some of these facts, so that they will be recorded in Hansard and so that
June 30, 1987

Supply-Trade and Commerce we will have an official statement of what has transpired with regard to the amount of money expended and the attendance at the fair. Then the minister, from his greater knowledge of the whole operation than is available to me, may wish to mention some other aspects which he considers important. He might indicate what he believes will be the permanent beneficial results from this great Canadian achievement.

Mr. Chairman, this particular item covers the Canadian participation through the Canadian pavilion only. The total amount voted for this is $21 million. I am glad to note that this is one of the projects at Expo which is operating within its budget. In this regard I think we must recognize the good work Mr. "Les" Brown has done, and I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre for his recognition of that. I believe the Canadian pavilion is a great credit to Canada. It is recognized as such by all Canadians who have visited it, and there have been fine and glowing tributes paid to it by visitors from abroad.
In respect of the broader picture of Expo itself, although it does not come under this item and I do not have all the facts and figures at my disposal for that reason, I should like to say a few words about it. I did refer to this earlier today, before the hon. member took his seat in the house. I said that the total attendance now exceeds 16J million people and is far in excess of the number which had been estimated up to this date.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The mere fact that so many people have visited the site has required the corporation of Expo to spend additional amounts of money, and this is increasing the requirement for capital. It was thought there might be a deficit of something in the order of $137 million in respect of Expo itself. It was hoped that the increased number of visitors through the turnstiles would increase the amount of revenue correspondingly. We still hope that will be the case, but to date it has not been, presumably because many of the visitors are from the local area, who come in in the morning and leave in the evening, without spending a great deal of money on the site. With the summer season now in full flight and increasing numbers coming from abroad there are indications that the amount of money left at the site per capita will increase. By whatever yardstick you use to measure, perhaps with the exception of a strict financial balance sheet approach, this is going to be a

great Canadian accomplishment and a great Canadian asset.
We are already concerned about the disposal arrangements for Expo. The master plan which was tabled some time ago indicated an amount of some $74 million which the C.C.W.E. hoped will be realized through salvage and the disposal of assets. We have established a committee under the tripartite governments-federal, provincial and city-to make recommendations to the Corporation of the World Exhibition as to how these assets can be disposed of to the best advantage, and the amount budgeted actually realized.
Hon. members will recall that under the terms, the participating countries are required to remove their buildings from the site, and leave the site in good repair unless other provisions are made. A number of nations have indicated they would like to contribute their buildings, and the mayor of Montreal has indicated he would like to have some of them. This, together with the other arrangements for disposal on winding up in due course, are under consideration. It has already been agreed that La Ronde, which is the amusement area, will continue in operation for a period of some two years under the tripartite arrangement. I expect to bring legislation before parliament in the fall seeking authority to continue participation in this operation for a period of two years, after which it is the intention of the federal government to dispose of its share of the assets, presumably to the city of Montreal.
I am sure we all agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre that this is a great success, and with the compliments he paid to the commissioner general, Mr. Pierre Dupuy, the assistant deputy commissioner, Mr. Andre Kniewasser, and to the chief engineer, Col. Churchill. There was one man he omitted to mention, because he was referring only to those with previous government service. I refer to Mr. Shaw, the deputy commissioner general, who has been a tower of strength in making a success of Expo. He has made a great contribution around which the whole program has in great measure revolved.

Mr. Speaker, I merely want to say to the minister that I am sure all members of the committee extend their congratulations to him and to his department, and to those who have been responsible for the unqualified success which has attended Expo. I have talked to many people who have visited almost all the world fairs over the years, and
June 30, 1967

one of them said to me that this is the greatest fair he had seen in his lifetime and the greatest he ever expected to see. This is a fine tribute to all those, including the minister, who have planned and carried out this very large undertaking. If Canadians ever suffered from an inferiority complex, this ought to dispel it.
It is only natural, living beside the country which has the most advanced technology in the world, that there are times when we wonder whether we can do things on as grand a scale, with as much success and with as much flamboyancy as our United States neighbours. Certainly Expo has demonstrated that the governments of Canada, federal, provincial and municipal, in co-operation with the business community and the general public, when they have a common purpose to achieve can do great things together, and Expo is a living example of that type of accomplishment.
We have only seen part of the picture and I think the summer months will add even more lustre. There will be bigger crowds, and before the end of the season I am sure Expo will be far beyond the finest expectations of all of us, including the minister.
At a time like this when we are having a party it is bad manners to ask how much it cost, but I should like to ask the minister two questions for the purpose of clarification. He mentioned the world exhibition and said the total cost was to be something like $21 million.
That is for the Canadian pavilion.

Is this amount covered under vote 29? I noticed the figures for the fiscal years 1964-65, 1965-66 and 1966-67 amount to just about $29 million. I think we have already spent $14 million. Will this total amount cover the entire cost?
Yes, I understand this will cover the entire cost. The $21 million should be adequate to cover the operation.

The other question I should like to ask relates to Expo itself. The minister mentioned something about an anticipated deficit. I think he referred to a short fall this morning, which is a much nicer way of expressing this situation. He suggested the deficit would be $137 million. He also referred to an amount of $74 million as a salvage and disposal value. Has this amount already been subtracted before calculating the anticipated $137 million deficit, or will that deficit be 27053-139
Supply-Trade and Commerce reduced by $74 million, if we are able to realize that amount?
No, we have assumed that there will be $74 million recovered through salvage and disposal of assets in the calculation of that $137 million figure.
So the $137 million will be the deficit after we have recovered the $74 million, assuming we are able to recover that amount?
That is a correct observation, Mr. Chairman.

We have a few minutes left, Mr. Chairman, and perhaps the minister
June 30, 1967

Supply-Trade and Commerce would deal with another matter. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics is another vital factor in the operation of Canada's economy. Very considerable alterations and improvements have been going on in the Dominion Bureau of Statistics over the last few years, because of the realization that is abroad as to its valuable work and the need for enlarging it. We have a few minutes left, and I wonder whether the minister would tell us something about that bureau, which has done such good work in the past.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I would be glad to say a word on behalf of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, which I think is one of the finest organizations of its kind in the world. I am constantly amazed at the volume and the broad sweep of information collected and disseminated by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. Hon. members might note that a great percentage of the answers in reply to questions asked on a wide variety of subjects comes through this organization. The subjects range from the consumption of snuff in Canada to the number of whales caught in the north Atlantic ocean.
One might almost say that the bureau has been in a constant state of growth because of the pressure of the demands that fall upon it from various departments. Last year it undertook the census, and this required a considerable amount of extraordinary expenditure. But it was done expeditiously and well. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics is endeavouring to computerize its operations and it has done so to a very large extent. The bureau has a very fine computer operation which enables it to get out the information required quickly. They are constantly working toward accelerating the pace with which information is made available, because the value of any information depends, (1) upon its correctness and (2) upon the speed with which it is made available to those who use it.
This information is made available to the consuming public of Canada, the various trade associations, provincial governments, and many others. The bureau has a wide variety of users and it is important that this information be made available expeditiously and correctly. We are spending a great deal of time and effort in building the bureau into the kind of organization that can meet those tests.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate what the minister said with regard to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. I notice
(Mr. Churchill.]

that there has been a growth in the bureau over the years. I am wondering whether there is any way of assessing how much of this growth results in increased benefit to the taxpayers, and how much of the growth in what we might generally term the public service-and I include all branches of the public service-is due to Parkinson's law. Of course, we have to recognize that this is a complicated age and there is a greater and greater demand upon public services of various kinds. These services can be of great benefit and no doubt are of great benefit, but sometimes I am appalled by the fact that we are told that because of automation, new electronic gear, and all this sort of thing, a service becomes very much more efficient, but the net result is that it costs more to provide that service.
I should like to mention an example of this sort of thing. The Minister of Transport made a very attractive statement the other day with regard to the telephone service of the government. A new system was evolved in the last year or so, and every call that is made is costing the taxpayer less money. Nevertheless there has been a very considerable gross increase in the cost of telephone services to, I think, practically every department of government. The answer to this of course is: Well, the government has become much more efficient and the departments use the long distance telephone service much more frequently than was the case when it was more expensive. It is also said it is much more efficient to make a long distance telephone call than it is to write a letter. But there is no evidence that there is any reduction in the cost of the traditional means of communication. We seem to go on and on in this way.
I would like to think there is a very close examination of the necessity for and value of any new service that is provided. I hope I am not misunderstood. I am all for providing every service that is reasonable for helping the economy and the general development of our country. But I think we have to be selective on occasion. I believe we have to select the things that give the greatest benefit for the money spent on them. There will undoubtedly be occasions when we cannot afford certain things, in the sense that they are not justified in the circumstances, and if as a result of deciding that we are to have a wide collection of attractive things the cost to the taxpayer continues to rise at a greater rate than the general growth of our country.
If this trend were to continue indefinitely, the tax burden would become heavier and
June 30, 1967

heavier. This growing tax burden will have exactly the opposite effect on our economy, our ability to compete in world markets and raising the standard of living for all Canadians, because if all these costs are passed on to the consumer-and it is inevitable that they are, in some form or another-the cost of living will go up and therefore for a given income the standard of living will go down.
I do not wish to create the impression that I hold the view that the Dominion Bureau of Statistics is particularly guilty or vulnerable in this regard. I assume that under the present minister a very careful watch is kept on a tendency to empire building, if you want to put it crudely.

Mr. Chairman, I have just one comment to make to the minister. I wonder whether he has read the report of the joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate and the recommendations of the committee in connection with the service provided by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. This committee ran into a problem all through its hearings. The problem was that the items relative to the price of food were weighted with this, that and the other thing in such a way that nobody, not even the economists, could give a true comparison with market fluctuations.
One of the recommendations was that the service of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics in this particular field should be overhauled and speeded up, and the reports brought out so that they were readily understandable by the general public. I wonder whether the minister has any comment in this regard.

No, Mr. Chairman, other than that we are striving toward that end. As I mentioned, as always there is the demand for the earlier presentation of this sort of material. I have not read the report in full but I have seen references to it. To the extent that the Dominion Bureau of Statistics can improve its efficiency and update its making available of information, we will try to do this.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
May I say in reply to the hon. member for Queens that we have been taking a good look at the growth to which he referred. I have been spending a fair amount of time on this point recently, together with the officials of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics and Treasury Board, to see to what extent Mr. Parkinson has been at work there. There has

been pressure from other departments requiring information and it is a problem for Treasury Board and the other departments to screen out what is essential. Once it is set out for the D.B.S. as a program approved by Treasury Board or by the government, it is up to the D.B.S. to render the best service it can with their program. The selection of programs is not its primary function; that is a matter for determination by the government, but if these things are not carefully watched there is a danger of Parkinson's law being applied to full effect. subtopic: MEASURE TO COMMEMORATE LANDING IN CANADA
MEASURE TO COMMEMORATE LANDING IN CANADA
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-7, respecting the observance of Leifr Eiriksson day.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-7, respecting the observance of Leifr Eiriksson day, is a very short bill. The explanatory note says that:
-the purpose of this bill is to commemorate the fact that Leifr Eiriksson was the first European to land on what is now Canadian soil.
I am not asking the government to declare a national holiday but merely to declare a Leifr Eiriksson day to commemorate or give recognition to the fact that Leifr Eiriksson was the first European to land on that part of North America which is now Canadian soil.
On September 3, 1964, the president of the United States, Lyndon B. Johnson, issued a proclamation designating October 9, 1964 as "Leifr Eiriksson day", in recognition of the discovery of North America about the year 1000 A.D. In view of the fact that the United

June 30, 1967
Leifr Eiriksson Day
States has seen fit to declare a Leifr Eiriksson day, it would be only appropriate that Canada do likewise.
I have suggested that the first Monday in August be recognized as Leifr Eiriksson day. My reason for suggesting that day is that on that day the annual Icelandic celebration is held at Gimli, Manitoba. Manitoba has the largest Icelandic settlement on this continent, and Leifr Eiriksson being of Icelandic descent I felt that this would be an appropriate day. The implementation of this suggestion would not cost the people of Canada any money; it would, however, give recognition to what is now known as factual history. That is the important issue.
I wish to read a short article from the Canadian Press which appeared in the Saturday, June 10, 1967 issue of the Winnipeg Tribune. Under the heading "Ontario Displays Vinland Map" it says:
The Vinland map said by Yale university scholars to be proof that Canada was discovered by Norsemen at least two centuries before the voyages of Columbus will be on display at the Royal Ontario Museum for three days next week.
The map, about 11 inches by 16 inches, was drawn on parchment about 1440 from source materials dating back to the 13th century voyages of Leifr Eiriksson, researchers say.
In the upper right hand corner is a large island labelled Vinland, with two river outlets thought to be the gulf of St. Lawrence and the Hudson straits.
This is the same map as was referred to in an article in the October 11, 1965 issue of the Washington Post written by staff writer Howard Simons, in which he outlines that Yale University and British museum scholars had unearthed evidence that Leifr Eiriksson had discovered North America about five hundred years before Christopher Columbus. I would recommend this article for perusal by all those who are interested in history and the preservation of historic facts.
Another article which I would recommend for study entitled "Leifr Eiriksson Discovered America" is contained in the 1965 winter edition of the Icelandic Canadian. In the same edition there is an article entitled "Some Notes on Leifr Eiriksson's National Origin and the Source on Greenland and Vineland" written by Professor Haraldur Bessason. Mr. Bessason is professor of Icelandic at the University of Manitoba, and he has done a great deal of research on this subject.
The observance of a Leifr Eiriksson day will not in any way effect Canada's recognition of the sailings of John Cabot and Jacques Cartier, or the achievement of Samuel de

Champlain who was the first European to establish a permanent settlement in Canada.
I wish to quote from a letter written by Dr. P. H. T. Thorlakson to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), dated January 7, 1965, giving a brief account of the early Viking voyages of discovery and exploration to the western hemisphere, and a brief reference to the recent archaeological discovery in Newfoundland. It reads as follows:
Eiric Thorvaldson, more commonly referred to as "Eric the Red" because of the colour of his hair, was the first explorer and colonizer of Greenland. In the year 985 A.D. he sailed westward from Iceland on a voyage of exploration. Having selected the west shores of Greenland as the sites for new settlements, he returned to Iceland to arrange for the transportation of his own and several other families to this new land. It is recorded that 35 ships sailed from Iceland but only 14 arrived. Some were driven back, others were lost. With Eric's family was his famous son, Leifr, born in Iceland. Their family home in western Greenland was situated at Eiricsfjord and was called Brattah-lid.
Some 15 years later, Leifr was sailing from Iceland to Greenland to visit his father when he was driven off course to the westward and southward by strong winds. He landed in a country which, according to the available records, had never been reached before by Europeans. When he finally arrived at his father's home, he reported the discovery of this new land situated to the west and south of Greenland.
In the year 1007, Thorfinn Thordarsson-better known as Thorfinn Karlsefni, an Icelander who had married Gudrid, the widow of Eiric's son Thorstein, set out to explore and establish settlements in this new land. His expedition consisted of 160 persons and several ships. They sailed from Greenland towards the southwest. He sighted a barren land covered with flat stones, "Helluland" and further south he came to a wooded land, "Markland". He recognized both these lands from the earlier description by Leifr. Thence they sailed far to the south. Finally, on their starboard side, they saw a long coast line with a sandy shore indented with bays. A river entered the ocean at this point. Here they landed and set forth to explore the country. Inland, they gathered ears of wild grain and an abundance of wild grapes. This was Vineland (Wineland) the Good originally described by Leifr Eiriksson.
Thorfinn Karlsefni and his adventurous colonists stayed in this new country for at least three years. During the first autumn (1007) a son was bom to Gudrid, the wife of Karlsefni. The child was named Snorri. Many notable Europeans, including the celebrated Icelandic-Danish sculptor Thorvaldsen, trace their lineage to this first child of European blood born in North America.
In the year 1917 the Icelandic sculptor, Einar Jonsson, was invited to the United States by Dr. Henry Goddard Leach on behalf of Mr. Bum-ford Samuel. By the provision of her will, the late Mrs. Bumford Samuel established a fund which was to be used to erect statues of representative pioneers of America in Fairmont park in Philadelphia.
June 30, 1967



[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
As a result of this visit, a statue of Thorfinn Karlsefni, created by a gifted Icelandic sculptor, was placed in Fairmont park in 1918, to memorialize these early attempts at settlement and as a tribute to the first European pioneer in North America.
In a book entitled the "Life of Christopher Columbus" written by his son, Ferdinand, is recorded the visit of his father to Iceland in the year 1477, fifteen years before he landed in central America. In a letter from Christopher Columbus to his son, quoted in part only in this book, it is stated that the explorer sailed from Bristol, England to Iceland in February, 1477.
Historians believe that Christopher Columbus' decision to visit Iceland was no doubt made after he had read the works of Adam of Bremen, who was one of the most distinguished scholars of Europe in the eleventh century. Adam of Bremen had recorded the story of the propagation of Christianity in northern Europe. After describing conditions in Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Iceland and Greenland, he stated: "The same king (Svend Estridson) also informed me about the discovery of one more region in that ocean-a region named 'Vinland', because grapes grow there spontaneously, produces the best wine; and corn too, without being sown in abundance."
This book, written by Adam of Bremen, was published between the years 1072 and 1076 in the manner that books were published before printing was invented.
The early discovery, explorations and attempts at colonization of North America, were memorialized by the government of the United States when they presented a statue of Leifr Eiriksson to the people of Iceland on the 1000th anniversary of the founding of the Althing-parliament-in 1930.
Canada, I believe, has now a most cogent reason for officially acknowledging the first recorded discovery of North America by designating an official "Leifr Eiriksson day". For the first time, we now have a day which has great significance to these early events and to our Canadian history. In September, 1964, a pierced stone weight used in spinning was unearthed in the northermost tip of Newfoundland at I'Amse aux-Medows. The discovery on Canadian soil of this soapstone spindle whorl indicates that the early Viking settlers included women, corroborating the accounts of the early Viking settlements along our eastern seaboard which are recorded in the ancient Iceland sagas. The day of this discovery may appropriately be chosen by Canada as "Leifr Eiriksson day" but no doubt other days of the year should also be considered.
A plaque, a centennial gift to Canada was presented by Canadians of Icelandic descent on April 14, 1967, and placed in the new library and Archives building in Ottawa. I just want to quote from the Winnipeg Free Press for Saturday, April 15, 1967. The article is headed "Plaque Marks Canada's Discovery" and states:
Prime Minister Pearson unveiled a bronze plaque in the new national library and Archives building here Friday as a centennial gift to Canada by citizens of Icelandic descent.
Dr. P. H. T. Thorlakson of Winnipeg, president of the Canadian Icelandic centennial committee, presented the plaque to commemorate discovery of
Leifr Eiriksson Day
the eastern coast of Canada by mariners of Iceland and Greenland in the late tenth century.
Mr. Pearson said the plaque "makes us more conscious than ever of the varied origins of our national existence."
He said it is now well established that the first discoverers of what is now known as North America were Vikings long before Christopher Columbus, John Cabot and Jacques Cartier came.
Noting on the trilingual plaque that Icelandic is the most economic language in the number of words used, Mr. Pearson jokingly suggested he would like to see it adopted as the official language of the House of Commons.
The plaque shows an open book and quill recalling work of Icelandic scholars who preserved eleventh and twelfth century records, and a replica of a Viking ship, along with two historic excerpts from The Saga of the Greenlanders, first written in Iceland about 1200 and preserved in a vellum manuscript.
Part I records the sighting of the new land by Bjarni Herjolfsson of Iceland in 986. Part II describes the voyage of Leifr Eiriksson some years later and his landing on Vinland-part of the coast of North America.
The heading on this plaque is, "A chapter of Canadian history-discovery of the western hemisphere". The introductory paragraph at the top of the plaque reads as follows:
This plaque commemorates the discovery of the eastern coast of Canada by mariners from Iceland and Greenland in the late tenth century.
The historic excerpt reproduced below is from Graenlendinga Saga (The Saga of the Greenlanders) first committed to writing in Iceland about A.D. 1200 and preserved in Flateyjarbok (The Flatey Book) a vellum manuscript compiled in Iceland about A.D. 1390.
Part I records the sighting of new land in the west by Bjarni Herjolfsson, of Eyrar, in Iceland in A.D. 986.	'
Part II describes the voyage of discovery of Leifr Eiriksson some years later and his landings in Helluland (Flatstoneland), Markland (Woodland) and Vmland (Wineland). These explorations led to an attempt at colonization by Thorfinnr Karlsefni, whose son, Snorri Thorfinnsson, was born on this continent.
Archaeological research in western Greenland and eastern Canada supports these ancient Icelandic records of exploration and colonization.
In conclusion, by the acceptance of this plaque, the government of Canada has recognized that mariners from Iceland and Greenland were the discoverers of the east coast of Canada and, indeed, of North America. The United States has given recognition to the fact that Leifr Eiriksson was the discoverer of North America and also that he was of Icelandic descent. I think it would be fitting if the government of Canada saw fit to recognize this historic fact in a similar manner.

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Matheson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: MEASURE TO COMMEMORATE LANDING IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Leifr Eiriksson is a symbol, a symbol of

June 30, 1967
Leifr Eiriksson Day
those adventurers whose spirit of inquiry defied danger and death. They are like the men who saw fit to climb Everest, a number of whom were lost, but finally Everest was conquered. The only explanation they could offer for their effort was that it was there. There was no greater purpose than adventure itself. These fierce Norsemen sailed the wild sea and discovered this land in which we live. I am reminded of these lines: Forth sped the Viking bold E'en through the Arctic cold,
On, ever onward ...
Three weeks we westward hove,
And when the storm was o'er,
Cloud-like we saw the shore Stretching to leeward.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stef-anson) is an excellent representative of his Viking ancestors. To him and to those pioneers who played a part in ushering in the drama of this new world, we say, "Skol". I believe in the importance of symbols, whether they be flags, shields or badges. I believe in heroes. I believe it was Carlyle who wrote of heroes and hero worship. Probably it is so that great ideas have been carried in the hearts of mankind by human example. Leifr Eiriksson is a symbolic hero as were John Kennedy, Winston Churchill and Pope John. They were all great human symbols.
Leifr Eiriksson has become part of the thought structure, the symbolism of the entire western culture. I believe that any great thought must be conveyed by some human life, even though the historic facts concerning that life may be uncertain and vague. I suppose, sir, on a day such as this all of us are thinking of that very special and precious human being who is a symbol to us and who is with us today. Her life has been a living symbol of service, from every call of duty she has never flinched, never wavered, like her brave father before her. I once saw her in uniform-a slip of a girl. It has been her glory to exemplify for her people honour and moral worth and we rejoice in her presence for our centennial celebrations.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I think it is interesting to remember that some of her ancestors, for several centuries, used the title "Dux Normannorum" or "Dux Normanniae". I am not clear when this practice was discontinued or whether in fact it is discontinued. It is interesting to note how these fierce Norsemen conquered successively France, Scotland and then England.
Leifr was the son of the great clan chief Eric the Red, who was referred to as the

strong and noble leader of the Norsemen. These stout hearts, with their great muscles, blond hair and blue eyes voyaged to the Faeroes, the Orkneys, the Hebrides, the coast of Normandy, to Iceland, Greenland, and even to Canada itself.
My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Stefan-son) who had the ingenuity to bring this motion before the house had every right to bring it. Before rising to speak I received a note from my good friend from Red Deer who will follow me, also of Scandinavian origin, in which he urges me not to talk against this bill. It would be hard for me to do so. My grandfather, John Matheson, was born in the northern part of Skye. His mother was Flora Nicolson-pronounced Nick-olsen. They spoke Gaelic. I am told that all these northern highlanders could easily understand Norwegian when it was spoken slowly. They were Vikings just a few generations removed. The Vikings were the people who-and no archaeologist and historian today can be precise as to where this was-somewhere around 1,000 A.D. touched down in our land.
I have read various historical accounts of these people and the comments by Samuel Eliot Morison, the great professor of American history. He suggests that relics such as the Kensington rune stone and the Beardmore weapons, which have been the subject of much research by archaeologists, are clumsy forgeries. I believe on the evidence now available he is wrong.
Notable European scholars, and here I am thinking of Paul Herrmann who wrote "Conquest by Man", suggest that there is much evidence, from artifacts of all kinds, to show that there were definite Scandinavian inroads very early in our history. I am intrigued by the account of Paul Herrmann, how in August, 1898, a Scandinavian by the name of Olof Ohman, in Solem near Kensington in Minnesota, discovered, by knocking his axe against a tree, a rune. I know that this matter has been the subject of controversy, but many people who are more authoritative on the subject than even the eminent Professor Morison is, regard this rune as evidence that Norsemen appeared in this land at an early time.
The stone spoke of a journey of eight Swedes and 22 Norwegians from Vinland. May I read the text of the runic inscription: (We are) 8 Goths (Swedes) and 22 Norwegians on (an) exploration-journey from Vinland over the West (i.e. through the western regions) We had camp by 2 skerries (i.e. a lake wherein are two skerries) one day's-journey north from this stone
June 30, 1967



We were (out) and fished one day Alter we came home (we) found 10 (of our) men red with blood and dead. Ave Maria.
Save us from evil
On the other side of the stone were chipped these words:
(We) have 10 of our party by the sea to look after our ships (or ship) 14 day's-journey from this island. Year 1362.
It is interesting to compare this date with the date of the attack on Rhodes and the early migrations of the Crusaders to the far east. It is interesting that there were then valorous men in armour on this side of the water. There are some suggestions that Bjarni, son of Herjulf, touched down in Canada perhaps a few years earlier. Certainly, as the hon. member for Selkirk has indicated, Lief stands above others and is the man worthy of being characterized as the symbol of this fearless and intrepid people.
Leifr Eiriksson, the Norse discoverer of North America, was probably born in Iceland. He was the son of Eric the Red, spent his youth in Greenland and in 999 A.D. visited Norway where he was converted to Christianity. He was commissioned by King Olaf Tryggvason to carry the religion to Greenland. According to "Saga of Eric the Red" in the collection of sagas known as "Hauksbok" it was on the return voyage from Norway to Greenland in about A.D. 1000 that Leifr Eiriksson, blown off his course, discovered hitherto unknown lands in which he found grapes, self sown wheat and a species of tree called Mansur.
He landed, secured specimens of this vegetation and continued on to Greenland where he was successful in introducing Christianity. There are various versions of this story but it is clear that the Norsemen from a very early period passed through some parts of our country-perhaps through the southeast corner of the United States, probably through Newfoundland.

It is interesting to note that archaeologists suggest that Bjarni Herjulfsson, while in his twenties, undertook the great voyage of 985 A.D. in which he navigated from some spot in western Iceland to this country and probably landed at, or saw first the flat landscape of Hamilton inlet in Labrador. After two days they sighted land anew-high mountains and
Leifr Eiriksson Day
glaciers, as in Greenland. They had sighted the southern part of Baffin island.
The Heimskringla records that Bjarni reported the voyage to Eric the Red, the uncrowned king of Greenland and that Eric's oldest son, Leifr, bought the ship from Bjarni and obtained a crew of 35, and the consent of his father, Eric, for a new voyage of exploration. Unfortunately, Eric had a fall from his horse; as a result it was left to his great son to take on the responsibility of that voyage of discovery. Thus Leifr discovered Vinland-a land laden with vines and grapes.
We do not know where Vinland is. We do not really know at what point on the coast Leifr landed. It may have been Massachusetts, but also, possibly, it may have been Virginia, Florida, New England or Newfoundland. The winter frost was so light that the grass had scarcely withered. In any event, it is clear from the evidence of the artifacts that from early years the Norsemen touched down on our shores. I see my hon. friend nodding his head; I should add that from early days the brave Irish, too, may have explored these parts.
While on the subject of where Leifr Eiriksson landed it is interesting to note that in Mallorytown, Leeds, in my constituency, they have been working under water for about a year and a half on what is believed to have been a British gunboat of about the year 1812. It is a flat lapstreak vessel. Though all the experts suggest that the boat is a British gunboat about 150 years old, and it has been studied by our northern affairs people for many months, my private theory is that it is Leifr's boat. Of course I may be wrong.

The importance of this bill is that Canada is a country of rich ethnic variety. Her Majesty was reminded of this variety when she saw the talent on the hill this afternoon-Ukrainians, Chinese, French, Estonian, Italian, Indian, German; one could go on-yes, and Jewish. All this is evidence of the contributions which have been made by people of many races-Africans, Slavs, men and women of both oriental and Caucasian descent.
Some writers theorize on this. Roy Matthews in an article which I would commend to hon. members entitled "Canada, The International Nation," says we must not get trapped in a bicultural and bilingual set-up which relegates others to third class status. Hon. members will appreciate that I am speaking today as a Norwegian.

The way to avoid such a prospect, in my view, is to ensure that the dilemma does not take on the form of a bilateral confrontation. Diversification is the secret: and this is the essence, again, of my plan for an "international nation." I would never imagine that Canada could escape from its unique situation vis-a-vis the United States; the relationship with our huge southern neighbour will always be paramount in our affairs and my scheme is shaped to recognize that fact implicitly. Likewise, I have no intention of suggesting that the special position afforded the English and French groups under Confederation should be weakened; I accept this factor as a valuable part of our Canadian heritage. What I seek to do is to weave these relationships into a wide and more satisfying design without in any way reducing their significance.
This respect for all has been eloquently expressed in a series of speeches by Her Majesty. She has sought always to encourage the best in us, not only in her realm of Canada but wherever in the world she is recognized as head.
In northern mythology there are three Norns or goddesses who are regarded as dispensers of fate. They are Urdur, the past- and perhaps we have been too preoccupied with Urdur in Canada-there is Verdandi, the present-and ours is a challenging present, and we would not change it for any other day-and there is Skuld, the future.
To the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stef-anson) and to all the strong people from northern lands who have enriched this country we say, God bless you, and may there be many more in Canada in the years ahead by natural increase and, I hope, by immigration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because I should like this bill to pass, my remarks will be brief. I think it is fitting and appropriate that at this time when we are thinking of the history of our land in a special way we should have speeches this afternoon about a particular aspect of our history, namely the occasion when the first European found himself on the shores of what is now our land.
I think it is fitting that we should take note of the background of our history, and it seems to me that what the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson) asks is little enough, namely that one day in our calendar should be known as Leifr Eiriksson Day. I should like to support this bill not only because of the link it suggests with the history of 900 or a thousand years, but also because in my view it is fitting

for us to recognize the great contribution to the life of Canada which has been made by Canadians of Icelandic descent.
I come from a part of this country where we are particularly aware of this fact. Indeed, all over Canada there are Icelanders and people from Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Finland who have made a valuable contribution to the life of Canada. But in my part of Canada we are particularly conscious of what people of Icelandic origin have done in helping, along with people of other origins and with all of us who are here, to build this land into the one we are celebrating just now, as it becomes 100 years of age.
For these two reasons, because of the respect it shows for an important aspect of our history, and because of the recognition it gives to people of Icelandic descent in this country, I should like to see the house accept the bill proposed by the hon. member for Selkirk.
I am interested in the fact that the bill does not ask for a holiday in the sense that it would be another day on which people would be free from work. However a most interesting day has been chosen, namely the first Monday in August, which is already celebrated as a holiday in terms of freedom from work in many parts of the country, under the name "civic holiday".
I hope it will not sound like a commercial on my part if I point out that I myself have a bill on the order paper, Bill No. C-57, which seeks to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code to provide that the first Monday in the month of August shall be a holiday, along with the others listed in the Labour (Standards) Code. I did not attach any name to that suggested holiday when I put it in my bill. I have received a number of suggestions as to what it might be called; perhaps it could be given a number of names. Anyway, I see no reason at all why both these bills should not be passed. Let us have a holiday in terms of freedom from work on the first Monday in August every year, and I see no reason why that holiday should not be called Liefr Eiriksson Day.
I have pleasure in supporting the bill introduced by the hon. member for Selkirk.

I rise to support this bill with a good deal of sentiment. As a descendant of some of the early pioneers in our land who came originally from Norway I have a strong family tie with the Nordic background of Liefr Eiriksson.
June 30, 1967

I would remind the hon. member who has just spoken, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), whose support for this bill I appreciate, that while Liefr Eiriksson was born in Iceland it was his father, Eric the Red, who first colonized that island in 970. Those Norwegian adventurers, seeking more productive lands, who discovered Iceland and settled it, went on further to Greenland and then further still to the eastern shores of Canada. Thus, Liefr Eiriksson not only has ties with Iceland, where he was born, but with the Nordic adventurers who came from Norway and who were the real discoverers of the new world of which Canada is today such an important part.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I think it is significant that this bill is being discussed today on the eve of Canada's centennial. I cannot think of anyone more worthy to sponsor it than the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson). On a day when we are considering the history of our nation relating to the 100 years just about to end, it is good that we should look further back into our past and identify the beginnings of our history.
I also appreciate the scholarly presentation which the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) has made. I do not want to be repetitious but I think it would be good to add a little detail to his remarks so that we may have on record more detail of how Leifr Eiriksson came to be the first Canadian of Scandinavian stock to reach what is now Canada.
The story of the life of Leifr Eiriksson falls into three parts. First came his Atlantic trip from Greenland to Norway in 999 A.D. He had gone to Greenland with settlers from Iceland. His father, Eric the Red, was the key leader in that adventure. As I say, in the year 999 A.D. he returned to Norway where, as the hon. member for Leeds has already stated, he came to know the king of that country but, more important than that, he came into contact for the first time with Christianity and became a Christian.
The second phase of his life follows his discovery of what he called Vinland, North America, in the year 1003 A.D. Following this discovery he returned to the Norwegian colony in Greenland and spent his life in stewardship there from 1004 to 1065 A.D.
These Norsemen were the first Europeans to leave their coastline and venture into uncharted seas. As their homeland was not, and still is not a rich land, 70 per cent of it being
Leifr Eiriksson Day
covered by mountain, glacier and moor, they went abroad seeking new lands with which to enrich themselves.
It was on the island of Iceland that Leifr Eiriksson was born in the year 970 A.D. Some ten years later his father founded the Greenland colony. Neither Iceland nor Greenland were a very great improvement upon their native land of Norway, so they continued to seek adventure farther away. Considering this, it is not strange to find in the story of Leifr Eiriksson that when he was 20 years of age he went back to Norway and, as I have mentioned, went to the court of King Olaf and came into contact with Christianity. From there he returned to Iceland, and later landed on the eastern coast of Canada.
It was a really astonishing performance. Although it is true that the hulls of the boats of these early Vikings were masterpieces of naval architecture, they were open, and they could only sail before the wind. They depended on oars to face into the weather, and also for a great deal of their propulsion. No craft was more than 50 foot long.
Whereas Christopher Columbus crossed the southern Atlantic, the Vikings sailed the Arctic without benefit of compass. They steered by the stars and by the birds. Having discovered this land in the year 1003, in the following spring they returned to Greenland. One can imagine the rejoicing and the jubilation in that colony of a few hundred souls when Leifr Eiriksson returned. It is no wonder they christened him Leifr the Lucky.
Today general recognition is advancing of Leifr Eiriksson as the discoverer of Canada and the western world. His voyage to North America in the year 1003, and then later the colonizing expedition of his brother, who set up the first colony of 160 people, are things which are now becoming established as facts of history. No one has done more to establish those facts than Professor Helge Ingstad of Norway, who himself has done much of the archeological work in Newfoundland, which has turned up the evidence of that first colony through artifacts directly related to that early period in history.
Today there are many people who believe that Columbus' discovery nearly 500 years later was directly due to the voyages of Leifr Eiriksson. At all events the Norsemen's claim to the original landing seems to be accepted. So, Mr. Speaker, I believe that we should seriously consider accepting this bill today so that there might be one day in the year, such

Leifr Eiriksson Day
as that suggested by the hon. member for Selkirk, that would give recognition to the first European to land in Canada.
Such an act would not only be fitting but would also be encouraging to our students of history and to all our young people, helping them to pay more attention to the great historic heritage of this country. Therefore I give my support to this bill. I agree with those who have already spoken on it, that it would be very fitting for the house at this time to give approval to it and thereby officially set a day in the calendar to be known as Leifr Eiriksson Day.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to see this bill passed and therefore will be very brief. We are known by our heroes and I think it is fitting that today, the last day in our experimental first 100 years, we officially recognize one of the great heroes of the western world, Leifr Eiriksson.
Canada has made a great contribution as a melting pot of nations to this top part of North America. We have no great errors to live down. This experiment which is now 100 years old has been a success, and I join with the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) in hoping, nay in praying that we will not bog down in any bicultural or bilingual quarrel, but that we will use this great experiment of the last 100 years to move forward into the next 100 years and prove that the experiment is only beginning.
The town of St. Paul in northeastern Alberta, embracing the three great cultures prevalent in that area, is the most successful centennial town in Canada. I only hope that here we can add one more tribute to the many heroes we have had by following the lead of the hon. member who has proposed this bill.
There has been much talk about symbolism this afternoon. I think it is rather significant that the number of this bill is C-7, the number of stars in the great dipper which was such a great boon to navigators. If we pass this bill it will be a tribute to an individual hero, a man who did not take his lead from the mob, a man who stepped out on his own, who expected help from nobody, and made the whole world a better place in which to live. Therefore I join with others who have spoken in saying that this bill should be given second reading.

Mr. Speaker, I greatly appreciate, as a French Canadian from Quebec, this opportunity to say a few words here tonight on Bill No. C-7, an act respecting the observance of Leifr Eiriksson day. Under this bill, the first Monday in the month of August would be known and observed as Leifr Eiriksson day throughout Canada.
Personally, I sincerely wish that this bill can be passed tonight, since Leifr Eiriksson is the man who, in all likelihood, according to old relations of the Scandinavian people, was the first to set foot on American soil.
Why observe Leifr Eiriksson day? What can Canada get out of it? I realize that there are in this house more descendants of that great people than I expected, of that ancient people that settled Iceland first from the Scandinavian countries, Sweden, Denmark and especially Norway.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stef-anson) who introduced the bill is a direct descendant, through his parents of Icelandic settlers. He might be also a descendant of Sigurd Stefanson who probably was a surveyor, a very able geographer at that time, taking into account the facts known to the men of those days because, unless I am mistaken, Sigurd Stefanson who probably was a survey-peans who prepared a chart of the North Atlantic on which appear the Scandinavian countries of Europe, and those countries Leifr Eiriksson called Helluland, Markland and Vinland.
Our Scandinavian compatriots, descendants of the ancient Vikings, are perfectly justified, as we all are, to be proud of their forebears. When it occurred to me that I might speak on this bill, memories of things I had read came back to me and, in the last few hours, I took the opportunity to refresh my memory a little on such epics, souvenirs of the gruelling voyages undertaken by these kings of the fiords, the heads of families and clans as were the Vikings, knowing that in those days every Norwegian family owned its own fiord and defended it with all the strength and the valour of its brawn and heart.
Descendants of the Scandinavian peoples are justified in their pride for their ancestors and we can understand that they are proud to promote this project of observing Leifr Eiriksson day.
